Prune the components of a Random Planted Forest

Source: R/prune.R
prune_components.Rd

Drops the small components of a forest's functional decomposition and, optionally, refits one coefficient per kept component. The rule and the threshold are chosen out of bag by default, from the forest itself without refits, or by K-fold cross-validation on the training rows. By default every kept interaction of three or more predictors is then coarsened so that it can be shown in at most max_panels heat maps, and the model is pruned again.

Usage

prune_components(
  object,
  data,
  y = NULL,
  ...,
  max_panels = 10,
  rule = c("D", "R"),
  tau = c(0, 1e-04, 3e-04, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1),
  select = c("1se", "min"),
  select_by = c("oob", "cv"),
  folds = 5L,
  fold_id = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  nthreads = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  keep_forest = FALSE
)

Arguments

object

[rpf]: A fitted rpf model (regression or classification).

data

[data.frame | matrix]: The training data of object, in the order of the fit: the predictors as passed to rpf() as x, or the data of the formula or recipe interface. For a formula or recipe fit, data may contain the outcome.

y

[numeric | factor | NULL: NULL]: The outcome of the training rows (the factor for classification). Required unless data contains the outcome of a formula or recipe fit.

...

Reserved for future expansion. Unknown arguments are an error.

max_panels

[numeric(1): 10]: The display: the most heat maps a kept component of three or more predictors may need; such a component is coarsened to at most max_panels heat maps, and the model is pruned again (see Details). A whole number of at least 1, or Inf for no display (the first pruning's model).

rule

[character: c("D", "R")]: The rules to consider: "D" drops, "R" drops and refits one coefficient per kept component.

tau

[numeric: c(0, 1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1)]: The thresholds to consider, as shares of the variance of the prediction (0.01 = 1%), each at least 0 and below 1.

select

[character(1): "1se"]: How the pair is chosen: "1se" (the largest tau within one standard error of the lowest RMSE) or "min" (the lowest RMSE).

select_by

[character(1): "oob"]: How the candidates are scored, and R's coefficients fitted: "oob" (out of bag, from one purification of object and no refits) or "cv" (K-fold CV with refits of the forest; R's coefficients in sample); see Details.

folds

[integer(1): 5]: The number of folds, used if fold_id is NULL: of the CV, or out of bag of R's refit and of the SE.

fold_id

[vector | NULL: NULL]: The fold of every training row: a vector of length nrow(data) with at least two distinct values. If NULL, the rows are assigned to folds folds at random (after set.seed(seed)).

seed

[integer(1) | NULL: NULL]: The seed set before the random fold assignment and, for the CV, before every fold's refit. If NULL, one is drawn from the current random number stream and stored in the result, so that the choice can be reproduced. The caller's random number state is restored afterwards (see Details).

nthreads

[integer(1) | NULL: NULL]: Number of threads for purifying the forests (object, and the CV's fold fits) and for the fold fits. NULL uses the nthreads object was fitted with. The result does not depend on it.

verbose

[logical(1): FALSE]: Report the progress of the choice.

keep_forest

[logical(1): FALSE]: Whether the pruned model keeps the forest object in fit. By default it keeps only the forest's description (you still have object): the model predicts from the components it keeps and is plain R data, which saveRDS() stores as it is. TRUE keeps the forest, as rpf()'s keep_forest.

Value

An object of class rpf_pruned, a list with elements:

  • fit: the description of object (its blueprint, mode, params, and with n_splits = NULL its oob_path and splits_oob), without the forest (fit$fit is NULL), so that a use of the forest from it is an error that says so. With keep_forest = TRUE, object as it was (not purified by the pruning).

  • rule, tau: the chosen rule and threshold.

  • intercept: alpha (the forest's intercept f_0 for "D"); for classification one per score column of the forest (K - 1 for multiclass loss = "logit", against the first level; with "exponential" and rule "R" the first is 0). predict_components() and print() report them as one per class, centred.

  • beta: named vector of the coefficients of the kept components (all 1 for "D"). For "R" with select_by "oob", intercept and beta are fitted on the out-of-bag components (see Details).

  • sets: the predictor sets of the kept components, as column indices.

  • components: a data.frame of every nonzero component of object on the training rows (after a second pruning of the display, only of those the first pruning kept: see below): component (its name, as in predict_components()), order, share, kept, beta (NA if dropped), and model_share: the share of the final model's component, Var(beta_S f_S) / Var(prediction of the model) on the training rows (with the display, of f_S in its heat-map form; for classification, as share, over the centred score columns; NA if dropped). share is what tau thresholds; model_share is the component's importance in the model, which print() shows. As the components need not be uncorrelated, the shares need not sum to 1.

  • oob: NULL unless the pair was chosen out of bag; otherwise a data.frame with one row per candidate: rule, tau, oob_rmse (corrected; used for the choice; 0 where the correction exceeds the uncorrected MSE, see Details), se_mse (from its per-fold MSEs), oob_rmse_raw and se_mse_raw (uncorrected), n_kept, min and one_se (the two choices). Its attribute n_rows is the number of rows with an OOB family.

  • cv: NULL unless the pair was chosen by CV; otherwise a data.frame with one row per candidate: rule, tau, cv_rmse, se_mse (SE of the CV MSE), n_kept (mean over the folds), min and one_se.

  • select, select_by, fold_id, seed: as used (fold_id and seed are NULL if no choice was made). For a given rule and tau, select_by is "oob" if R's coefficients were fitted out of bag, otherwise NULL.

  • criterion (classification only): "brier" or "logloss", what the candidates were scored by.

  • With the display (finite max_panels) and a component coarsened, a second pruning runs, and these describe it: its candidates are the components the first pruning kept, with the coarsened ones in place, and oob is its table. components then lists only these components, and their share (which the second pruning's tau thresholds) is of the variance of their model (the intercept plus these components) on the training rows, not of the forest's prediction; every nonzero component of object with its share of the forest's prediction is in display$first$components. Without a coarsened component, they are the first pruning's. With the display, components also has form ("full" for one or two predictors, "asis" if its own cut points need at most max_panels heat maps, "coarsened"; NA for a component of three or more predictors the first pruning dropped, so only without a second pruning) and heat_maps. The element display is a list: max_panels; first, the first pruning's model (without fit); coarse, per coarsened component (named as the components): S (all the component's predictors), C (the coarse predictors, |S| - 2 of S: the panel predictors), q (the numbers of intervals aimed at; merged ties can leave fewer, lengths(cuts) + 1), cuts (per coarse predictor), cells (the number of heat maps, prod(lengths(cuts) + 1)), var_kept (the share of the component's variance kept), forest_panels, kept (in the final model), candidates (every candidate's coarse set, q, cells and variance kept), stored (what prediction needs; no training data) and seconds (the time to choose and build its form); asis, per component kept as it is (form "asis"), its panels with the same names and meaning: S (all the component's predictors), C (the panel predictors: the |S| - 2 of S with the fewest own cut points; of ties, the first in S), cuts (per predictor of C, its own cut points: the leaf bounds of the trees containing S inside the range of the training values), forest_panels (prod(lengths(cuts) + 1)) and kept; forms, per component of three or more predictors the first pruning kept, its form, heat maps and variance kept; second (whether a second pruning ran); seconds (the time of each step); cache, an environment holding the coarsened components' search indices, built at their first predict() (a cache, not part of the model: rebuilt when missing or invalid, as after saving and loading). In coarse and asis alike, a panel is a cell of cuts (a value x of predictor k of C lies in cell findInterval(x, cuts[[k]])), shown as a heat map over the two predictors setdiff(S, C) at full resolution.

  • store: the pieces of the kept components that are not coarsened, from which the model predicts (see Purification), and cache, an environment holding them built for prediction.

Use predict() and predict_components() on it. Without its forest, save it with saveRDS(); with it, with rpf_marshal() (which works either way).

Details

The forest is decomposed into its purified components f_S, one per set S of predictors (see purify() and predict_components()), at all orders up to max_interaction, and its intercept f_0. The size of a component is its share of the variance of the prediction f on the training rows, share_S = Var(f_S) / Var(f). The shares are descriptive sizes, not a partition: the components are not orthogonal on the data, so they need not add up to 1. A component is kept if its share is at least tau (and it is not identically zero on the training rows). Two rules are available:

  • "D" (drop): the prediction is f_0 plus the kept components. rule = "D" with tau = 0 is the unpruned forest.

  • "R" (drop and refit): the prediction is alpha + sum(beta_S * f_S) over the kept components, with the intercept alpha and the coefficients beta_S by least squares of y on the kept components (the minimum-norm solution if the components are collinear). The components themselves are not changed, only their scale. With select_by = "oob" (the default, see below), the least squares use each training row's out-of-bag components instead of the forest's own, for a chosen and for a given rule and tau. The forest's own components have fitted the training rows' noise, so least squares on them scale the components up (on California housing the three-way interactions by about 1.3, where new data wants about 0.9). With select_by = "cv", and where the default falls back to it (see below), the least squares use the forest's own components on the training rows.

The choice. If more than one pair of rule and tau is given (the default: both rules and the grid 0, 0.01%, 0.03%, 0.1%, 0.3%, 1%, 3%, 10%), the pair is chosen by its out-of-bag (select_by = "oob", the default) or cross-validated ("cv") RMSE. With select = "1se" (the default), the largest tau whose MSE is within one standard error of the minimum is chosen (the SE is the standard deviation of the per-fold MSEs of the minimum, divided by sqrt(K)), and at that tau the rule with the lower RMSE. With select = "min", the pair with the lowest RMSE is chosen (ties, up to a relative 1e-12: the larger tau, then "D"). "1se" gives sparse models: with "R" fitted out of bag the out-of-bag error changes little over a range of tau, and "min" keeps small components that add nothing on new data.

Out of bag (select_by = "oob"). Every tree family of object is grown on a bootstrap sample of the training rows, and the purification works family by family. So every family's components (see Purification below) are also evaluated at the training rows outside its bootstrap sample. A row's out-of-bag (OOB) component is the mean over its OOB families (about 37% of them), and its OOB intercept likewise. The purification uses the predictors of all training rows, not the outcome, so no outcome information of a row enters its OOB components.

  • The kept components of every tau are those of the final model (the shares of object on the training rows).

  • "D" is scored by the OOB intercept plus the kept OOB components.

  • For "R", alpha and beta_S are fitted as for the final model, by least squares on the OOB components, but only on the rows outside each of K folds (folds, fold_id, seed). They are scored with the OOB components of the fold's rows, so that no row scores coefficients fitted on it. The final model's are fitted on all rows with at least one OOB family.

  • An OOB mean averages m_i families (about 37% of B = n_families), the final model all B, so the OOB prediction scatters more around its expectation. The OOB MSE is therefore corrected: per row it subtracts (1 / m_i - 1 / B) * v_i, with v_i the across-family variance of the candidate's prediction, estimated from the OOB means over the even and over the odd families (for a row whose OOB families are all even or all odd: the mean estimate of the other rows). Without the correction, the noise of the OOB components makes the candidates look worse than they are. The uncorrected values are reported as oob_rmse_raw.

  • If the correction exceeds a candidate's uncorrected MSE, its corrected MSE is reported as 0. That is not a perfect candidate but an overshooting, unreliable estimate (it happens with very few rows, e.g. "R" with about as many coefficients as rows, or with almost no noise). Such candidates are not chosen, unless all candidates are at 0 (then they tie).

  • The OOB RMSE is taken over the rows with at least one OOB family, the SE for "1se" from the per-fold MSEs.

  • With few families the OOB means average only one to a few families, and many rows have none (16% at 4 families). In a simulation (p = 6, n = 800, 60 replicates) the corrected OOB error of the unpruned "D" was within 1.5% of the test error at 4, 10, 20 and 50 families, that of "R" within 4.4% except once (+11.5% at 10 families with a 3-way interaction), and the OOB choice was as good as the CV's or better from 10 families on (within 0.4% in test error, or better by 7-10% where the CV's fold fits choose poorly). Below 10 families (n_families), the default select_by scores by CV instead (with a message); an explicit select_by = "oob" warns.

  • A deterministic forest has no out-of-bag rows, and a forest restored by rpf_unmarshal() from a blob made by an earlier version has no in-bag counts (with a message): with the default select_by, they are scored by CV instead.

  • A given rule "R" and tau (no choice) is fitted on the OOB components too, with the same fallbacks: below 10 families or without in-bag counts its coefficients are fitted in sample (with a message), and so they are for a deterministic forest. A given "D" needs no OOB components.

  • Factor predictors are coded by the outcome of all training rows: their levels are ordered by the mean outcome (regression), by the share of the second class (binary classification) or by the first principal component of the class proportions (three or more classes; Coppersmith, Hong and Hosking 1999). So a row's own outcome enters the coding its OOB families split on: with factors the OOB error is somewhat optimistic.

Cross-validation (select_by = "cv"). For each fold, the forest is refitted with the parameters of object on the other folds (after set.seed(seed), the same for every fold), its components, shares and refit are computed on those rows, and every candidate is scored on the held-out fold. The CV RMSE is sqrt(sum(SSE_k) / n), summing the squared errors over the K folds.

The chosen (or given) pair is then applied to object itself (not refitted): its components and shares on data, and for "R" the least squares on the OOB components of data's rows (out of bag) or on its components on data (by CV). data and y must therefore be the rows object was trained on, in the order of the fit (checked).

The display (max_panels, default 10; Inf switches it off). A component of two predictors is one heat map. A kept component f_S of three or more predictors is shown as heat maps over two of its predictors, one per cell of the others. If its own cut points need more than max_panels such heat maps, it is coarsened:

  • Two predictors of S stay at full resolution. Each other predictor k is cut into q_k intervals of equal numbers of training rows (ties merged), with prod(q) <= max_panels; q_k = 1 averages k out. Only the maximal q vectors (no q_k can grow) are considered; they are listed directly, not searched among all max_panels^(|S| - 2) vectors.

  • Within a cell, f_S is averaged over the coarse predictors with the product of their training marginals. The coarsened component is not purified again: purify() identifies the components under the joint distribution of the training rows, not under the product of the marginals, and the averaging changes the component's means along its two full-resolution predictors and its mean over the training rows. It is used as it is (no part of it is moved into the intercept or into components of lower order).

  • Of all choices of the two full predictors and the q vector, the one keeping the largest share of the variance of f_S on the training rows is taken (ties: the first in lexicographic order).

Then the same rule prunes again, on the components the first pruning kept, with the coarsened ones in place of the originals. Its shares, which tau thresholds, are of the variance of that model (the intercept plus these components) on the training rows, not of the forest's prediction. A pair chosen out of bag is chosen again out of bag, with the same candidates and folds, scored with each family's coarsened components at its out-of-bag rows (R's coefficients out of bag); a given rule and tau, or a pair chosen by CV, is applied again as it is (R's coefficients out of bag if the first pruning fitted them so, else in sample; a CV choice is not repeated, as it would need the display in every fold's refit). The prediction then uses the coarsened components, so the pruning judges the model that is shown. In simulations (48 data sets) this second pruning had 0.49% lower test error than pruning and then coarsening, and 0.57% lower than not coarsening; on California housing (50 families, order 3) the default keeps 30 components, shown in 75 heat maps. If no kept component needs coarsening, the model is the first pruning's. The display costs about as much again as the out-of-bag pruning: a purification restricted to the components being coarsened (two at a time) for their candidates, and one for their out-of-bag values; the stored coarsened components take a few MB each on 16,000 rows at order 3, more at higher orders.

Purification. The pruning needs every component's values at the training rows (and out of bag, its OOB means), not the purified forest: purify() keeps every component of every tree family as pieces, which at high orders takes far more memory than the forest (see Cost). So each family is purified in turn, as purify() does (mode 2, all orders), its components are evaluated at the training rows and added up, and the family's pieces are freed. The pruned model then stores the pieces of its kept components only, merged over the families exactly as purify() stores them, and predict() and predict_components() evaluate them from there; a coarsened component (the display) is stored in its coarsened form. The components equal those of the purified forest up to rounding (about 1e-15 relative), and the stored ones are the purified forest's bit for bit. object itself is not purified: an earlier purify(), at any maxp_interaction or mode, is left as it is and does not change the result.

Random numbers. The folds are drawn after set.seed(seed), and the CV's fold fits after it too. Afterwards the random number stream is restored to its state on entry (after drawing seed if it is NULL), so the call does not reset the caller's stream.

Cost. The out-of-bag choice purifies the families of object once (see Purification); it needs no fit. The CV fits and purifies the forest K more times (each fold's forest as purify() does). Only the components the forest has are evaluated (at most sum(choose(p, seq_len(max_interaction))), usually far fewer: the subsets of the trees' predictor sets). The memory is the forest's plus about n doubles per component, three times that for the out-of-bag choice, plus one family's components at a time per thread; storing the kept components passes over the families once more. On California housing (16,512 rows, 200 families, n_try_split_points = 3, share_candidates = 0.1, the fast draw, 8 threads; measured when this column pass was added) the whole call of rpf(n_splits = NULL, prune = TRUE) peaked at 2.3 GB of physical footprint (4.1 GB of resident memory, RSS) at order 3, and at 6.4 GB (9.9 GB RSS) at order 8 (all predictors), most of it the 31 coarsened components the display keeps; there purify() alone needs more than 12 GB of RSS. nthreads speeds up the fits and the purification.

Classification. A classification forest is pruned the same way, with its scores: one for a binary outcome, one per class otherwise. Every component then has a column per class, and:

  • A component's share sums its variance over the classes' scores, centred across the classes (as predict() reports them with type = "link": the part all classes share does not count), over the same sum for the prediction. One kept list serves all classes. (Internally loss = "logit" fits K - 1 scores against the first level; centred, the shares, the criterion and the model do not depend on which level is first.)

  • "R" fits one coefficient per kept component, shared by the classes, and one intercept per class (up to a constant shared by the classes, which the probabilities ignore; they are reported summing to 0), out of bag as for regression.

  • The criterion is the forest's loss's own: for loss = "L1" or "L2" the squared error of the raw scores summed over the columns (the Brier score; least squares for "R"), for "logit" and "exponential" the log-loss of the probabilities that predict(type = "prob") makes (maximum likelihood for "R", by Newton's method from rule "D"'s model). The OOB correction is its second-order form (see rpf(), "Classification"). The tables then have oob_loss, se_loss, oob_loss_raw and se_loss_raw (the mean criterion) instead of the RMSE columns, and cv_loss and se_loss for CV; select = "1se" uses the SE of the mean criterion. A binary forest with "L1" or "L2" has one 0/1 column and is pruned as a regression forest of that response, with the RMSE columns.

  • The display coarsens a component with one form (C, q, cuts) for all score columns, chosen by the variance kept of the centred columns; its stored form is one per score column.

  • predict() takes type as predict.rpf() does, and predict_components() has one column per component and class, named as for the forest (<component>__class:<level>); with "logit" or "exponential" each component's columns, and the intercepts, sum to 0 across the classes.

See also

predict.rpf_pruned(), predict_components(), purify(); rpf() with prune = TRUE fits and prunes in one call.

Examples

# A main effect and a pure interaction
set.seed(1)
x <- matrix(runif(600 * 4, -1, 1), ncol = 4, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:4)))
y <- x[, 1] + 2 * x[, 2] * x[, 3] + rnorm(600, sd = 0.3)
fit <- rpf(x, y, max_interaction = 2, n_families = 20, n_splits = 50, prune = FALSE)

# Rule and threshold chosen out of bag (no refits): the largest tau within one SE
# of the lowest error
pruned <- prune_components(fit, x, y, seed = 1)
pruned

#> Regression. Prediction = intercept + the sum of 2 components.
#> Intercept: -0.00482281

#>  x1        44%

#>   The forest: 20 tree families of 50 splits.
#>   From the forest's 10 nonzero components (purified): those with a share of at least 10% of the forest's Var(prediction), each with one coefficient, fitted out of bag (rule R).
#>   Rule and threshold chosen by out-of-bag error (1-SE rule; 5 folds, seed 1) among 16 candidates.
#>   Left out: 8 components, shares together 2.1% (largest x2, 0.65%).

# A given rule and threshold: no choice; R's coefficients are still fitted out of bag
prune_components(fit, x, y, rule = "R", tau = 0.01)
#> ── Random Planted Forest model ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Regression. Prediction = intercept + the sum of 2 components.
#> Intercept: -0.00482281
#> 
#> Components (largest first), importance = share of the variance of the prediction on the training rows:
#>  component importance
#>  x2:x3     58%       
#>  x1        44%       
#> 
#> How it was chosen:
#>   The forest: 20 tree families of 50 splits.
#>   From the forest's 10 nonzero components (purified): those with a share of at least 1% of the forest's Var(prediction), each with one coefficient, fitted out of bag (rule R).
#>   Rule and threshold given.
#>   Left out: 8 components, shares together 2.1% (largest x2, 0.65%).

predict(pruned, x[1:5, ])
#> # A tibble: 5 × 1
#>    .pred
#>    <dbl>
#> 1 -0.768
#> 2  0.563
#> 3 -1.18 
#> 4  1.07 
#> 5  0.101

# A three-way interaction, shown in at most 4 heat maps
y3 <- x[, 1] + 4 * x[, 2] * x[, 3] * x[, 4] + rnorm(600, sd = 0.3)
fit3 <- rpf(x, y3, max_interaction = 3, n_families = 20, n_splits = 100, prune = FALSE)
shown <- prune_components(fit3, x, y3, max_panels = 4, seed = 1)
shown
#> ── Random Planted Forest model ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Regression. Prediction = intercept + the sum of 2 components.
#> Intercept: 0.0509343
#> 
#> Components (largest first), importance = share of the variance of the prediction on the training rows:
#>  component importance

#> How it was chosen:
#>   The forest: 20 tree families of 100 splits.
#>   From the forest's 14 nonzero components (purified): those with a share of at least 10% of the forest's Var(prediction), each with one coefficient, fitted out of bag (rule R).
#>   Rule and threshold chosen by out-of-bag error (1-SE rule; 5 folds, seed 1) among 16 candidates.
#>   Left out: 12 components, shares together 11% (largest x2, 2%).
#>   Components of three or more predictors in at most 4 heat maps each, then rule and threshold chosen again on these (R, tau = 10%; none left out).
#>   Heat-map forms: x2:x3:x4: x4 in 4 intervals (95% of its variance)
shown$display$forms
